profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting between the clinical lead and the claims-review lead for a qualitative study of closed malpractice claims involving diagnostic error in ambulatory care. After double-coding the first 25 claims, the team has noticed repeated disagreement about whether the electronic health record contributed to the error, which diagnostic process step should be tagged as the main breakdown, and why seemingly similar claims are being classified differently. The agenda is to diagnose the source of the coding inconsistency, review a few representative discordant cases, and decide on a practical fix for the next coding round. The expected outcome is an agreed plan for re-review and codebook refinement so the remaining claims can be analyzed more consistently.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.role: Principal Investigator and Ambulatory Diagnostic Safety Researcher
members.expertise: General internal medicine, diagnostic error research, qualitative coding of clinical cases, outpatient workflow analysis
members.background: An academic internist who leads a patient-safety research group and has previously studied missed test results and referral failures in primary care EHR environments.
members.private_state: She wants the study to capture workflow-mediated EHR contributions, not just overt software malfunctions, and is worried that a narrower reading will undercount how much the EHR shapes ambulatory diagnostic breakdowns.
hidden_assumptions: An error can be 'EHR-related' even if the software technically works as designed, as long as inbox routing, result visibility, documentation structure, or message handling within the EHR shaped the missed diagnosis.

The relevant 'diagnosis date' is the earliest point at which the record contains enough abnormal information that a reasonable clinician should have acted, not necessarily the date of formal pathology confirmation.

When someone says they will 'review the claim file,' that includes the full de-identified dossier with chronology, expert reports, exhibits, and any attached audit-log materials, not just the summary abstraction sheet.
The 'pulmonology missed nodule case' refers to the 2019 claim involving an abnormal CT routed to a primary care inbox and no documented follow-up.

members.name: Daniel Cho
members.role: Senior Claims Analyst and Risk Management Nurse
members.expertise: Closed malpractice claims review, legal chronology reconstruction, diagnostic event abstraction, ambulatory risk management
members.background: A nurse risk manager who has spent a decade abstracting malpractice files for insurer and hospital reviews, with a strong habit of aligning coding decisions to what is explicitly supportable in the legal record.
members.private_state: He wants the coding scheme to remain conservative and defensible against legal records, and is concerned that broad interpretations of EHR contribution will make the dataset feel subjective.
hidden_assumptions: A case should be coded as 'EHR-related' mainly when the record shows a direct EHR function issue such as template-driven omission, routing configuration, display problem, or documentation artifact, rather than any general workflow failure that happened while using an EHR.

The relevant 'diagnosis date' is when the diagnosis becomes formally established or communicated in the claim record, often pathology confirmation or explicit documented diagnosis, because that is the most defensible legal anchor.

When someone says they will 'review the claim file,' that usually means the standardized de-identified claim summary packet used for abstraction unless someone specifically requests exhibits or technical appendices.
The 'pulmonology missed nodule case' refers to the 2020 claim involving a specialist note that was finalized late after an incidental lung finding.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say a claim is or is not 'EHR-related.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means any diagnostic breakdown materially shaped by the EHR-mediated information environment, including inbox management, result visibility, note structure, or electronic referral messaging, even if the system did not malfunction.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a narrower class of cases where the claim file supports a direct EHR-function contribution such as routing setup, interface display, templated documentation effects, or other concrete system-linked artifacts.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both participants routinely use the same research shorthand and both view their meaning as the obvious one for this study, so the phrase feels fully shared and does not trigger clarification.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'pulmonology missed nodule case' they mean
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the pulmonology missed nodule case' as a representative discordant claim.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the 2019 outpatient CT claim where an abnormal lung nodule result landed in the primary care in-basket and follow-up never occurred.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the 2020 specialist claim where the incidental finding was described in a pulmonology note that was signed and routed late.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The dataset contains several very similar lung-nodule claims, and the shorthand label sounds specific enough that each assumes the other is recalling the same file.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both talk about 'when the diagnosis was made' or 'how long the delay was.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 anchors the delay to the earliest clinically actionable evidence in the record, such as the first abnormal imaging result that should have triggered evaluation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 anchors the delay to the first formally established diagnosis in the legal chronology, such as biopsy confirmation or explicit documentation of cancer.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Using a single timeline point is a normal abstraction practice, and both participants think they are simply applying the standard chronology, so the different thresholds remain implicit.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to 're-review the claim file'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they should 're-review the claim file' on discordant cases.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the re-review includes the entire available file, including exhibits, chronology, expert opinions, and any attached audit-log details that might reveal information-flow issues.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the re-review is limited to the standard abstraction packet already prepared for coding, unless a special request is made.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both have a stable local workflow in their own roles and use the same phrase for it; because re-review sounds routine, neither thinks to define the file boundary explicitly.

turns.inner_thought: The disagreement rate is higher than I expected because I think we're undercalling EHR-related cases whenever the software didn't visibly fail. For this study, the EHR contribution includes inbox routing, result visibility, note structure, and messaging patterns that shape follow-up. If we code only obvious malfunctions, we'll miss the real ambulatory diagnostic safety signal.
